title: Once Interrupted Give It Your Full Attention
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This piece offers a counterintuitive response to workplace interruptions, arguing that once focus is broken, the smartest move is often to give the interrupting person or issue full attention rather than trying to immediately resume the original task. The reasoning rests on a specific claim about attention recovery. The piece frames this as serving two goals at once, it eliminates the root cause of a second interruption, and it sends team members a message that their issues genuinely count. The recommendation is bounded to interruptions substantial enough to break deep focus.
points: Since it takes several minutes to fully re-engage after any interruption, that recovery window can be repurposed toward attending to the interruption instead of resisting it.
Giving full attention to an interrupting colleague often prevents a second interruption by fully resolving the underlying need.
The recommendation sends a clear relational signal that other people's issues genuinely count.
The piece bounds the advice explicitly to interruptions substantial enough to break deep focus.
quotes: Once interrupted while engaged in a task, it takes several minutes to fully reengage and become hyper-focused on the task at hand.
Forty-five minutes of deep work, where leaders can attend exclusively to a task, is the very definition of productive time.
Once interrupted, it often makes the most sense to give the source of the disturbance your full attention.
This attention often prevents another interruption in the short term, as fully answering the question or attending to the need eliminates the root cause for the interference.
You might find it is even more important than the task you’re working on. In that case, you’ve made a great leadership call.
